current_episode.title: The Otago Opportunity - Episode 20 - Student Politics

guest.bio_context: Flynn Nesbit is a second-year law student at the University of Otago, originally from Mount Maunganui, who is also pursuing a Bachelor of Arts with studies in criminology and potentially Māori studies. He was the first first-year student elected to the OUSA executive in 30 years, and previously ran a humorous mayoral campaign for Dunedin under the Silly Hat Party in the local government elections. His political interest stems from family background, including his grandmother who is a lawyer and active union member in the TEU.

pending_qa.q: What is the ACT Party's proposed policy on student service fees and why do student associations oppose it?
pending_qa.r: ACT proposed making student service fees opt-in on a service-by-service basis, allowing students to choose which services to fund individually rather than paying a collective fee. OUSA opposes this because students already pay the service fee to the university regardless of membership, and fragmenting funding would make it harder for student associations to provide essential services that all students rely on.

pending_qa.q: What are the main tenant and rental issues affecting students in Dunedin according to student union advocacy?
pending_qa.r: Healthy home standards are virtually unenforceable with huge backlogs, landlords can exploit the rental market because they know students will need housing despite poor conditions, tenancy tribunal is a costly and lengthy process with limited resources, and the government recently reintroduced no-cause evictions which empowers landlords to wait out the year knowing another tenant will arrive.

pending_qa.q: What are the key policy positions that a student union executive campaigned on?
pending_qa.r: Flynn campaigned on reversing voluntary student membership to make it automatic again, campaigning for fees-free education, implementing rental warrant of fitness standards, providing paid placements for students, and winter energy payments. The executive has also focused on ethical investments and expanding OUSA's engagement on these issues.

pending_qa.q: How has OUSA demonstrated increased student engagement and organizing capacity?
pending_qa.r: OUSA organized two of the biggest student protests on fees since the 1990s, held a leaders debate with two body leaders that drew over 300 people—the biggest in 11 years—and successfully enrolled 500 people across just two days, while maintaining momentum on advocacy beyond election years.

pending_qa.q: How do student unions decide which political issues and causes to take positions on?
pending_qa.r: The accountability mechanism comes through elections, feedback, and the student magazine Critic holding the executive to account. Student unions work from what they campaigned on and general student sentiment. When multiple executives share a vision from the start and collaborate with other student groups, consensus is easier; when there are competing ideas, nothing gets done because too much energy goes into internal debate.

pending_qa.q: What advice would a student union leader give voters in a general election?
pending_qa.r: Support policies that benefit you now and all of us together, not policies designed to benefit only a few people in hopes of becoming one of them. When all of us are doing well, all of us are doing well, and there is more to life than working until death—a communal approach benefits everyone more than individualistic policies.
